analysis.one_liner: Makes federal agencies follow slower, cost-first procedures before issuing major regulations.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared the House Judiciary Committee 13-9 and was placed on the House calendar, but never received a floor vote and died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill rewrites the rulebook federal agencies follow when they issue regulations. Rules with big economic effects would need extra advance notice, public hearings with cross-examination, detailed cost-benefit studies, and agencies would generally have to adopt the cheapest rule that meets the law's goals. Companies could challenge agency findings in court more easily at every stage, and the White House regulatory office would gain power over agency decisions. Supporters said it adds transparency and discipline; the practical effect is that major protections — on pollution, workplace safety, consumer finance, and more — would take longer to issue and be easier to block or weaken in court.
analysis.who_benefits: Regulated industries — manufacturers, energy companies, financial firms, and others facing federal rules — gain the most. The bill gives them extra procedural hurdles to raise against rules, a default toward the least costly rule, trial-style hearings where they can cross-examine agency evidence, and easier access to courts to overturn rules. Law firms that litigate regulations would also gain a larger volume of challenges to handle.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Regulated industries and regulatory litigation firms

how_it_helps.text: Requires agencies to publish an advance notice of proposed rulemaking, at least 90 days before the formal proposal, for any 'major rule' (roughly $100 million in annual economic cost or more) or 'high-impact rule' ($1 billion or more), and to solicit public comment for at least 60 days [S3].

Requires agencies to adopt the least costly rule that meets statutory objectives, allowing a more costly rule only if the agency can justify the added cost by public health, safety, or welfare benefits [S4].
Requires a trial-style hearing with cross-examination before adoption of any high-impact rule, and lets members of the public petition for hearings on major rules [S3].

Expands judicial review: courts could no longer defer to an agency's interpretation, cost-benefit analysis, or guidance documents, and could immediately review interim rules issued without full notice procedures [S3].

Concentrates new authority in the Administrator of the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (a White House political appointee), whose guidelines on cost-benefit analysis would be entitled to judicial deference [S4].

analysis.who_pays: People who depend on federal protections would bear the cost if the bill passed: air and water quality rules, workplace safety standards, consumer financial protections, food and drug safety, and similar safeguards would take years longer to issue and would be more vulnerable to litigation. The bill's own definition of costs is broad, counting effects on jobs and competitiveness, but does not require equally rigorous accounting of the benefits of protections.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone relying on federal health, safety, and financial rules

drawbacks.text: Supporters argued current rulemaking can be slow, opaque, and costly, and that the bill adds transparency: advance notice, public hearings, electronic dockets, and required periodic review of major rules [S3].

Small businesses and other regulated entities said compliance costs from major rules can be significant, and cost-benefit analysis could help agencies pick rules that achieve goals at lower cost [S4].

The bill's 'least costly rule' default runs against statutes that put health and safety first, and would let companies relitigate an agency's science through cross-examination hearings and repeated court challenges, shifting the practical burden of proof onto regulators [S3].
The bill exempts Federal Reserve monetary-policy rulemaking from its cost-benefit and hearing requirements [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Some pieces — advance notice, electronic access to the rulemaking record, and periodic review of major rules — have genuine transparency value. But the bill's core effect is procedural delay and a cost-first default that conflicts with health and safety statutes. Under normal rules an agency's technical judgment gets some respect in court; this bill would invite companies to challenge every major rule's science and economics, and the practical result is that protections Americans rely on would be delayed, diluted, or dropped. The cost of that falls on the public, while the savings fall on the regulated companies.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee approved it 13-9 and placed it on the House calendar in September 2013, but party leaders never brought it up for a floor vote, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2015 [S6].

narrative.text: Bob Goodlatte (R-VA), the House Judiciary Committee chairman, introduced the bill on May 23, 2013 with 23 cosponsors, 20 of them Republicans and 3 Democrats [S5].
The Judiciary subcommittee on Regulatory Reform held a hearing in July 2013 and forwarded the bill to the full committee by voice vote [S6].
The full committee ordered the bill reported by a vote of 13-9 on July 24, 2013, and reported it on September 28, 2013 (H. Rept. 113-237), placing it on the Union Calendar [S6].
No floor vote ever occurred in the House, the Senate never took it up, and the bill expired at the end of the 113th Congress on January 3, 2015 [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, federal agencies kept their existing rulemaking authority and the people who rely on federal health, safety, and financial protections were spared the added layers of delay and litigation. Regulated industries, which had pushed for the changes, gained nothing from this Congress, though the approach resurfaced in later Congresses.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Agencies and people relying on federal protections

for.name: Bob Goodlatte
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and steered it through subcommittee and full committee markups to a 13-9 vote ordering it reported.

for.name: 23 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; 17 additional members joined as sponsors when it was reported in September 2013.

for.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce
for.what_they_did: Backed the Regulatory Accountability Act as a top legislative priority for reducing regulatory costs on business.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote; it sat on the Union Calendar for the remaining life of the Congress.

against.name: 9 House Judiciary Committee members
against.role: Committee members voting against reporting the bill
against.what_they_did: Voted no when the committee ordered the bill reported 13-9.

against.name: Public-interest and consumer groups
against.role: Opposing coalition (Public Citizen and allied groups)
against.what_they_did: Argued the bill would delay and weaken health, safety, and consumer protections and make it easier for companies to overturn rules in court.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was heavily one-sided — 20 of 23 cosponsors were Republicans — and the committee reported it 13-9; the bill never reached a floor vote where party breakdowns would have shown up.

industries.industry: Regulated industries (manufacturing, energy, finance, and others facing federal rules)
industries.note: The bill would give companies extra procedural weapons against rules, a default toward the cheapest rule, and easier court challenges. Their gain comes from delayed or weaker protections the public pays for.

Expanded judicial review, immediate review of interim rules, and cross-examination hearings would generate a large volume of new challenges to agency rules, and the cost of fighting rules would be borne by the public in delay.

Agencies would face required consultations with the White House regulatory office, hearing mandates, and expanded court review of their determinations, reducing their independent ability to issue protections.
